catalog_quote: [p.96] Accentuation in Carib is regular. The position of the accent mainly depends on the number of long vowels, diphthongs and VCC-sequences occurring in the word. From an accentual point of view there is a clear equivalence among these three. 1) If in a given word only one long vowel, diphthong or VCC-sequence occurs, then the accent always falls on the last vowel. ... 2) If two long vowels, diphthongs, or VCC-sequences occur in a word, the accent always falls on the second of these segments. As in 1), their position is irrelevant. ... [p.97] 3) If three long vowels, diphthongs, or VCC-sequences occur in a word, the second long vowel, diphthong or VCC-sequence bears the accent in 185 out of the 228 cases in my material. ... sweep_summary: gali1262 (Galibi Carib) has exactly one stress-keyword title in the sweep: Maxwell (1981), 'Über die rhythmische Natur des Wortakzents im Dyirbal und Hopi' (De Gruyter, DOI 10.1515/9783111355177.75). It is about Dyirbal and Hopi, not Carib; Glottolog record 403593 itself marks the Carib link as a 'computerized assignment from \"natur\"' (a machine false match on the German word Natur). The chapter is paywalled (De Gruyter Brill bot-blocks curl/web lookups; Crossref shows no license) and priority for acquiring it is none. No new source for Carib stress came out of the sweep, so the catalog's deciding source (Hoff 1968, weight-hedged) stands. As the best first-hand statement actually read, I re-read Courtz (2008) sec. 2.3.2 (already on file from the 2026-09-16 pass): Eastern Surinamese Carib has non-final alternating stress whose parity is set by initial-syllable weight, and Courtz states explicitly (fn. 92) that this differs from Hoff's Western Surinamese description — a dialect refinement, not a supersession. fetched sources records (Glottolog HTML/BibTeX, Crossref JSON, empty De Gruyter landing) and a record are in

new_statements.quote: Stress in words (except clitics) In words of one syllable, that syllable is stressed. In words of two syllables, the first syllable is stressed. In words of more than two syllables, even syllables except the word final syllable are stressed, if the word initial syllable is light. If the word initial syllable is heavy, odd syllables except the word final syllable are stressed. When there is more than one stressed syllable in a word, it is hard to say which stress is the stronger. [fn. 92:] The description of stress patterns in Carib differs considerably from Hoff (1968, 96-104). This may be explained by the difference in dialect: here, stress in Eastern Surinamese Carib is described, while Hoff describes stress in Western Surinamese Carib.
new_statements.citation: Courtz, Henk (2008). A Carib grammar and dictionary. Toronto: Magoria Books (Leiden University PhD; hdl 1887/12578). Section 2.3.2 'Stress', printed pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 40-41).
new_statements.reading: NOT a sweep item — the sweep's only title hit (Maxwell 1981) is about Dyirbal and Hopi. This is the strongest first-hand statement I actually read in this sweep, from the Courtz 2008 grammar already on file. Eastern Surinamese Carib: monosyllables stressed; disyllables initial; longer words show alternating stress that never hits the final syllable, with the parity set by initial-syllable weight (light initial -> even syllables, heavy initial -> odd syllables), and no clear primary among the stressed syllables. Weight of the initial syllable governs the alternation, which is compatible with the catalog's weight-hedged coding, but Courtz explicitly says his pattern differs from Hoff's (the catalog's deciding source, Western Surinamese Carib, where stress is placed by the count of long vowels/diphthongs/VCC sequences). So it refines the catalog record by adding a dialect split rather than contradicting or superseding it.

audit.recode_to: Two-tier record. STRESS: quantity-sensitive, bounded, left-edge iambic rhythm - disyllables initial; in longer words sigma2 (and sigma4...) stressed if sigma1 is light, sigma1 (and sigma3...) if sigma1 is heavy (heavy = diphthong or coda C, i.e. CVV-diphthong+CVC; no phonemic long vowels), word-final syllable never stressed, no single primary identifiable ('hard to say which stress is the stronger') [Courtz 2008:27-28 sec.2.3.2; length = exponent of stress, 2008:32, 38; = van der Hulst & Visch 1992 iambic feet; = Hoff 2014 'stress-bearing first foot', durational]. PITCH ACCENT (Hoff 1968:55, 96-102, W. Suriname): H on the second heavy/long counted from the left (= head of the second foot), else on the final vowel, free among non-first heavies when 3+; keep this verbatim as the accent rule with a caution that Hoff himself (2014) dissociates it from lexical stress and Courtz attributes the 1968-vs-2008 difference partly to dialect (W vs E Suriname). Also fix srule: iterating rhythmic (secondary) stress IS described (Courtz 2008:28 /atu_kupa_ra/, /ka_Nkasa_pa/; Hoff 1968's length alternation). If the catalog must keep one 'kind', code QS bounded left-edge (iambic) with caution, not weight-hedged unbounded.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all four quoted passages (pp.55, 96, 97, 101-102) are verbatim in the held OAPEN text layer of Hoff 1968 at the stated sections; page renders of pp.96/101/102 are also held. (2) Deciding source: a 440-pp reference grammar by the language's main describer with a dedicated, count-based accent section - authoritative for 1968 and still the fullest statement of accent placement; StressTyp2 rests on the same page. (3) But the record equates Hoff's pitch 'accent' with word stress, and two things seen today put that at risk: Hoff's own 2014 chapter (Crossref abstract read; full text paywalled) says Carib accent and lexical stress are dissociated, stress being durational and located in the first foot, the accent never falling on the stressed syllable; and the metrical literature fetched sources now (van der Hulst & Visch 1992, open access) plus Gildea as quoted in Yamada 2010 (fetched sources)

sources.quote: p.35: 'In feet of more than one syllable there is a point where the pitch rises markedly from one syllable to the next. The syllable after this rise is considered to bear a pitch accent... Within the foot it is possible for the accent to fall on the foot final syllable as in are:pá..., or on the prefinal syllable as in ja:kóno "friend", ihpo:rîri "creek"... In feet consisting of only two syllables, however, the pitch accent always falls on the final syllable as in pe:rú'; p.36: long syllables = V:, diphthong+:, or closed by h/nasal; all syllables short before pause. Examples pattern with Hoff'

sources.quote: p.131-132: 'the prosodic system in the language remains poorly understood... The phonetic realization of stress in Kari'nja is neither completely consistent nor completely predictable... The prosodic system has been described as an iambic system (c.f. Gildea, in press), but there are complications. The foot structure, which differs from primary stress, is organized in such a way that the head of a foot gets prosodic prominence... A heavy first syllable does not effect the iambic system - the heavy syllable forms a foot on its own and subsequent syllables continue predictable patterns'; p.19 qu

sources.citation: van der Hulst, Harry & Ellis Visch (1992). Iambic lengthening in Carib. Linguistics in the Netherlands 9: 113-124. DOI 10.1075/avt.9.12hul (open access).
sources.quote: p.113: 'According to Hoff (1968) each word in Carib contains an accent (manifested as high pitch), which is located on the second heavy syllable in the word (where V:, VC and diphthong count as heavy). If there is only one heavy syllable, the accent is on the final syllable.' Analysis (p.114): length distinctive in first syllable only; quantity-sensitive iamb; V:, VC, ViVj heavy; final syllable extrametrical; vowels in strong position lengthened; p.123: 'a rule like "head of second foot or final syllable" gives the right result' for accent. All data from Hoff 1968 (plus Hoff p.c.).

sources.note: Same author's later, pitch-measurement-based restatement: abstract says accent and lexical stress are DISSOCIATED in Carib, stress being the durational head of the first foot and the pitch accent never landing on it. Our 'weight-hedged / second heavy / unbounded' coding is Hoff 1968's pitch accent; this chapter decides whether that prominence is word stress at all or whether stress is left-edge first-foot (iambic).
